articles.title: Can gravitational fields break and reconnect? Einstein's equations suggest they can
articles.description: More than a century after Einstein first devised the equations that describe gravity, physicists are still finding new ways of interpreting them. Luca Comisso, an associate research scientist in Columbia University's departments of Astronomy and Physics and the Columbia Astrophysics Laboratory, and Felipe A. Asenjo of Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez in Chile, recently found a new way of looking at Einstein's equations that reveals a striking analogy with "magnetic reconnection" in plasmas, which occurs when magnetic field lines break and reconnect, powering explosive phenomena such as solar flares.

articles.title: Japan's genome-editing law sets a global ethics challenge
articles.description: A Hiroshima University researcher contends that Japan's newly enacted law regulating human genome-edited embryos and germ cells marks a significant advance in the governance of reproductive genome editing. Tsutomu Sawai, professor at Hiroshima University's Graduate School of Humanities and Social Sciences, praises the new law for defining prohibited activities and penalties for violation but also stresses the need for stronger international coordination to prevent the prohibitions from being circumvented by individuals seeking procedures abroad.

articles.title: Earth's ice ages may have been driven by a hidden ocean chain reaction
articles.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between Earth's opposite poles that may help explain how the planet plunged into past ice ages. New research suggests that as massive ice sheets expanded across the Northern Hemisphere, they cooled Atlantic Ocean waters that eventually traveled south toward Antarctica. This cooling may have disrupted Southern Ocean circulation, allowing the ocean to absorb and store more carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, further cooling the planet.

articles.title: Machine learning simulations reveal how plastic transforms into hard carbon
articles.description: In a new study published in Chemical Science, researchers from the University of Oxford's Department of Chemistry have used machine learning simulations to trace how a common polymer transforms into hard carbon, revealing the atomic-scale processes that give this technologically important material its disordered structure.

articles.title: What we owe our sisters, what we must demand of our brothers
articles.description: Ask my mother what sorority I'm in, and she'll say something about Pi Day. Ask my father the same question, and I guarantee you'll be left on read. Neither of them can tell you what a sorority is. But I can tell you that the first thing I learned wasn't a chant or a song. It was a sentence: Text me when you get home. A hair tie passed across a bathroom sink. A shoulder to cry on when your best friend suddenly passes. A hand at the small of your back, steering you out of a conversation before you've admitted you're uncomfortable. We learn it young, never formally in school, the way you learn the stairs of your own house in the dark. No one tells you why sisterhood matters until you need it. Misogyny is rarely a storm. It's a climate. We have survived in it long enough that we dress for the weather without noticing: the keys jammed between our fingers at night, the uneasy backwards glance, the hand over the drink, the apology we offer first so no one else has to. And when someone is hurt, we're cross-examined before we're believed. We're bombarded with questions of: What were you wearing? What did you drink? Why did you stay? Why didn't you scream louder? Why are you being so dramatic? I return to this every time I read the headlines. Jane Doe against Cornell University, and cases like it, are not surprises to any of the women I know. And yet even in the conversations "debating" misogyny, we somehow become the punchline. Sorority has become shorthand for shallow. And I'll admit, I believed some of it, too. Just one year ago, I would have associated sororities with parties, drinking culture or recruitment OOTD videos. Instead, I didn't have the most glamorous rush process. Unsurprisingly, I find that very few people do. Maybe you were disappointed by your options, or elated, or both within the same hour. We can never truly predict our outcome, but all of us ended up with something larger than life and larger than just ourselves: A sisterhood. Popular culture and Internet stereotypes will forever glorify college sororities as cutthroat, exclusive, catty and reinforcing an imaginary hierarchy. What I find is the opposite: women who lead, fight and rewrite history every day. Women who are bold disruptors with the kindest hearts I know. Women who clap louder for each other than for themselves, and who understand you can love someone while holding them to a standard of excellence. That's the whole premise of sisterhood, and it isn't the letters. It's choosing, again and again, to see the best in each other, and to support women in their pursuit of progress. My mother still asks if Pi Beta Phi is spelled like Pi Day. I tell her yes. Then I check the group chat to make sure everyone made it home. This portion of the piece is written by Siyeon Joo, Pi Beta Phi, a sophomore from Cade, LA, studying Molecular & Cellular Biology and Public Health. This sisterhood is worth celebrating, worth fighting for. The communities that promise us belonging and protection must also be willing to examine the ways they can perpetuate harm. We cannot celebrate the best of Greek Life without acknowledging its failures. For so long, women have carried the burden of facing a disproportionate level of harassment, assault and violence on college campuses. The 2019 Campus Climate Survey conducted by The Association of American Universities found that 1 in 4 undergraduate women experienced rape or sexual assault after enrolling in college. There is no denying that Greek life is strongly associated with higher rates of sexual assault, due in part to specific social structures, substance use and cultural attitudes leading to a lack of accountability within groups. A study conducted by the National Institute of Health have found that fraternity members are three times more likely to commit sexual assault than non-affiliated male students. Additionally, sorority women experience higher rates of sexual assault than non-affiliated female students. College campuses and Greek Life have created environments where women are placed in vulnerable positions and men act with depravity and harm women (Berger, n.d.). Or they do not act and are equally complicit. In October 2024, a Cornell student later identified publicly in court documents as Jane Doe alleged that she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity while intoxicated and unable to consent. According to a civil lawsuit she filed in September 2026, fraternity members discussed her in a group Snapchat chat in real time, referring to her as "free pussy" and asking whether the "shop" was still open. The perpetuation of rape culture, and sexual violence and harassment towards women continues because of passivity and the normalization of misogynistic social constructs. According to the National Institute of Health, alcohol misuse acts as a major risk factor for nonconsensual sexual encounters and unfortunately, many Greek social events provide access to alcohol, along with a space where heavy drinking is normalized. Additionally, fraternal subcultures can create peer-dynamics that encourage hyper-masculinity. This often manifests in control or objectification of women, competitive attitudes toward sexual conquests and a fear of speaking up (or "snitching") against their fellow brothers. The 50+ Chi Phi brothers at Cornell that failed to speak up show how these dynamics extend beyond the men who perpetrate sexual violence to the peers whose silence allows it to go unchallenged. We also recognize that sexual violence is not experienced exclusively by women, nor is it perpetrated exclusively by men. Men, too, experience sexual assault, harassment and unwanted sexual advances, including at the hands of women affiliated with Greek Life. These experiences deserve the same seriousness and accountability we demand for female survivors. While this article focuses on the role of fraternity culture in perpetuating sexual violence in light of recent events at Cornell, that focus should not be mistaken for a dismissal of other survivors. Regardless of gender or Greek affiliation, anyone who experiences sexual misconduct deserves to be heard and supported. Yet, we do not believe the answer is abandoning community. If anything, the failures of Greek Life have shown us how desperately women need one another. Sororities serve a special role on college campuses where women from all walks of life can have the opportunity to join one another in spaces that encourage growth, built-in support systems, and a collective understanding that sisterhood is there for you. Sisters protect and advocate for one another. Sororities encourage education and growth in academic and social settings. Greek Life is built around an incredibly powerful idea of loyalty. But that very same loyalty becomes dangerous when protecting the group becomes more important than protecting the people. Some of the structures that cultivate loyalty among men in fraternities may lead them to fail to report cases of sexual misconduct. Yet when these structures are formulated differently, they become sources of protection among women. Brotherhood and sisterhood never mean unquestioning allegiance to one another. They mean working together to create a community where we empower one another and intervene when something is wrong. If women are willing to ask more of ourselves and our sisters, we should be able to ask more of our brothers. Many men believe that because they do not harm women themselves, that they are doing enough. But that is not enough. Men remain complicit as they stand by as their friends, brothers, and even strangers reading degrading group chat messages, laughing at misogynistic jokes, even witnessing assault themselves, and, too often, do not act. If a brother has caused harm, holding him accountable is not a betrayal of brotherhood. It is brotherhood. We should not have to ask women to become experts in avoiding dangerous men while only asking men to promise that they are not those men. We should expect more from one another. We ask for you to look out for the women around you, but also the men next to you. We are not here to shame anyone, but to direct us all to our responsibility as students in Greek Life, and recognize the actions and inactions that continue to perpetuate harm. While this responsibility includes awareness and education, it extends to policy reform and new student conduct procedures. It requires men to believe they can be better and dismantle structures in which perpetrators are protected and those who challenge and dismantle norms are ostracized. For so many women, the words "text me when you get home" are second nature. They are a quiet acknowledgement of the dangers we anticipate. Of the responsibility we feel to protect one another. We dream of a day where those words are no longer said out of fear, where women do not have to rely on shared locations or the vigilance of their sisters to feel safe. But until then, we will keep asking our sisters to text us when they get home. And we will keep asking our brothers why we have to. Siyeon Joo is a sophomore from Cade, LA, studying Molecular & Cellular Biology and Public Health. Frances Leiter is a senior from Los Angeles, CA. studying Art History. Veda Kommineni is a sophomore from Edwardsville, IL. studying International Studies.

articles.title: YouTube has transformed basketball culture
articles.description: Viewers spend over 40 billion hours annually watching sports content on YouTube. That's over 4.5 million years of sports viewing on the platform... yearly. This statistic came as no surprise to me, because YouTube is what led me to discover the sport I love today. Here are some factors I believe have allowed YouTube content creation to reshape how fans experience and engage with basketball. 1. Engagement beyond the screen It's ironic that one of the first factors that comes to mind is the real-life engagement YouTubers bring to the table rather than the video production itself. As YouTubers reach a certain level of "celebrity" status, their interactions beyond the screen are what create positive feedback that drives deeper fan engagement. Whether it's inviting subscribers to join videos, doing local park takeovers, playing at the community gym, or hosting streetball showcases, these actions make creators' basketball experience feel more tangible for fans. These efforts also target local communities and the youth, such as coaching or building Amateur Athletic Union (AAU) teams and using their influence to support the next generation of players. 2. Testing the extremes Content creation becomes especially interesting when it is experimental, pulling the 'what if' scenarios that take a good amount of connections, investment and coordination. For example, basketball YouTuber sensation Jesser made videos like "1 NBA Star vs. 20 Top High Schoolers" or "Going to 5 NBA Games in 50 Hours." His videos often include a challenge or mystery element, with shocking prizes like "Make This Shot, Win $25,000!" By producing videos that spark questions, especially behind-the-scenes footage, exclusive tours at athletically renowned universities, player interviews, and courtside or on-court views and interactions, they keep fans on their toes. 3. Creating narratives Content creators I have watched use these compelling narratives about specific basketball scenarios or history, driven by suspense and revelations. They uniquely frame what seems like outdated content, bringing it back into conversations or highlighting new perspectives; they draw player connections and comparisons, pairing them with visually exciting edits to enhance the storytelling. I remember always being hooked by the open-ended titles, such as "I Have Never Seen a Star Fail Repeatedly Like This" or "There May Never Be Another Goat," by YouTubers MJ2KALLDAY and JxmyHighroller, respectively. Other videos emphasize a controversy or narrow it to one player's story, such as "The One Night LeBron James Wouldn't Pass" or "How Nike Lost Stephen Curry with ONE WORD." 4. So much to learn. As popular as basketball challenge and trick-shot videos are, many also offer skill demonstrations and practical advice. It is interesting how moves get adopted when something goes viral, and how younger generations especially use media like YouTube to mimic their favorite players' styles. I also personally loved watching basketball commentary when I couldn't stay up late to finish the game. Many creators go beyond that with in-game and player analyses, even recapping several games at once for playoff series play or uploading about a team's progression over the season. Significantly, when creators post reaction or opinion videos, they spark conversation. When viewers want different perspectives on a game or basketball debate, they can tune in or join the discussion in the comments. YouTube provides an accessible space to stay up to date on basketball topics and hear others' thoughts. It is refreshing when content creators are well-versed in the game's history and intricacies, not just skilled at playing it. 5. Versatility I see content-driven basketball as multifaceted in two main ways: first, on the basketball side, YouTube highlights different forms of the game, such as streetball, one-on-one, pickup basketball, dunking, different skill levels of organized play and highlights from around the world. On the YouTube viewership side, basketball can feel relevant and relatable because it connects to many other interests, including fashion (jersey designs and sneaker culture), music (player collaborations), gaming, artwork (court murals), science (statistics, strategic gameplay) and more. Content creators don't just collaborate with NBA players; notable professional players like Stephen Curry, Giannis Antetokounmpo, and Jared McCain also have channels, sharing vlogs that offer more insight into their lifestyles and fitness. YouTube was how I chose my first outdoor basketball, learned how to shoot and decided what drills to practice for hours in my driveway. It was how I learned the rules and moves well enough to try out for my 7th-grade team. Countless recaps, commentary and narrative uploads helped me familiarize myself with the NBA and the sport's lingo, fueling my growing passion. As it has shaped my relationship with basketball, I remain curious about how the boundaries of basketball content creation will continue to be pushed and redefined for emerging players and enthusiasts worldwide.

articles.title: Club Spotlight: Blue Jay Racing (Baja)
articles.description: Blue Jay Racing, or Baja SAE, is a student club in which members design an off-road single seat vehicle over the course of a year. The club is part of an organization called SAE International. Members spend the summer and fall designing the next year's car, the winter manufacturing the vehicle and testing it, and the spring and early fall competing. Recently, Blue Jay Racing retired its 2026 car. The leading purpose of Blue Jay Racing is to develop the engineering skills of club members. The team is primarily made up of Mechanical Engineering majors looking to gain experience in the field. Junior and Blue Jay Racing member Andre Hurst says the club is particularly useful for students hoping to go into the engineering industry after graduation. "A lot of what we do here is similar to the engineering that students will be doing if they decide to go into industry," said Hurst. "No one comes into Baja as a good engineer. The goal is that Baja turns you into a good engineer, and then you enter into industry as a good engineer." New member and junior Christian Nambo-Reyes emphasized the effort that older club members put in to teach those who have just joined. Although Nambo-Reyes has been enthusiastic about cars and their mechanics for years, this effort for inclusion did not go unnoticed by him. "They don't expect you to know anything. They teach you the basics, what they want you to do," said Nambo-Reyes. "They walk you through everything." This past year, Blue Jay Racing's car placed 4th overall in the 2026 season, where the group competed against around 200 international university teams under the Baja SAE umbrella. Each season is made up of three different four-day competitions: one on the East Coast, one on the West Coast and one in the middle of the country. In 2026, the Blue Jay Racing team traveled to Oregon in May, Rochester, N.Y. in June and Ohio in September. Each competition is made up of a series of events designed to test different components of the car. Over the first two days, the car doesn't drive at all. The focus of these two days is the cost report of the car, a breakdown on how much of the car was made in house versus outsourced, the design presentation, which consists of a report of all of the materials used and the reasoning behind this decision, the tech inspection, where the safety and integrity of the car are inspected, and a brake check. Once all the tests are passed, a car is allowed to compete. The Saturday of competition is known as "Dynamics Day," where the car competes in four driving tests: 100-foot acceleration time, the rock crawl, either a hill climb or sled pull and maneuverability. Sunday's highlight is the endurance test - a four-hour continuous race in which each team must fix problems with the car as they arise. Typically, the event consists of the 50 to 60 cars in competition racing wheel-to-wheel around a track. The car that completes the most laps over the four-hour period wins. In the Oregon competition, Blue Jay Racing's 2026 vehicle received first place in overall dynamics, second in acceleration and third in both the hill climb and endurance tests. Regardless of last season's success, the club has shifted its focus to designing its 2027 car. According to Hurst, this endeavor can take some members, especially club leadership, up to 40 or 50 hours a week. "It's for sure a lot of work," Hurst said. "It takes a lot of time and effort because we are learning how to engineer as we are building the car." For Blue Jay Racing members, though, this time commitment is worth it. It means gaining experience in the field, building something tangible and developing a network within the sphere of mechanical engineering. "It's very fulfilling to work on something for many hours, and then you finally get to see it manufactured. You can hold it in your hands," Hurst says. "It makes the hours and hours that I spend on this team worth it." According to Hurst, mechanical engineering is a field in which for undergraduates, grades matter far less than experience. Having the experience in Blue Jay Racing of hands-on work on a car is something that employers look for, he said. Additionally, Blue Jay Racing provides an alumni network of people who undergraduates can look to for internship or job opportunities. "They're usually happy to help because they probably went through four years of Baja," says Hurst. Another focus of the club is community. Because the team consists almost entirely of Mechanical Engineering majors, older Baja members can give the younger ones their thoughts on classes to take and general advice relating to the field as a whole. "I've gotten advice on homework, what classes to take, what electives to do, what professors to have, all that sorts of stuff," Hurst says. Nambo-Reyes agrees with Hurst as to the community aspect the team provides to members. "They've been very welcoming. They'll be here to help us out." Blue Jay Racing represents far more than just the design and construction of a vehicle by serving as a launchpad for the next generation of mechanical engineers. It serves as a way for budding engineers to gain experience in the field and push their knowledge outside of the typical classroom environment.

articles.title: The Nobel Prize in Physics 2026: insights into the importance of IceCube
articles.description: The Nobel Prize committee, carrying out its annual recognition of key discoveries and innovations in various scientific fields, recognized Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin-Madison for its prize in Physics this year. On October 6th, the institution announced the honor, citing Halzen's "decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin." In an interview with The News-Letter, Physics PhD student Andrew Mattson offered insights into the significance and science behind the committee's decision this year for the world of physics. Mattson's research uses techniques rooted in quantum sensing to detect gravitational waves in an attempt to search for dark matter - of which little is known or understood, other than that it has some effect on gravity and is unlikely to be made of the same components as normal matter like protons, neutrons or electrons. His research operates with the working theory that a new group of particles can help describe this behavior. The hunt for particles is what underpins the Nobel's decision this year to award neutrino research. Neutrinos are considered incredibly small and elementary particles that are only affected by weak nuclear forces and gravity, but not the strong force or electromagnetism. Their unique qualities have led to several proposed mechanisms and theories regarding their activity and potential to explain fundamental mysteries of the universe. The decay of radioactive isotopes is essential to our understanding of neutrinos. Mattson went on to elucidate the process resulting from instability within specific atoms. This could lead to several decay channels, of which the most relevant is the process of beta decay, where a neutrino and electron are emitted from the unstable atom. This led to the discovery of the neutrino thanks to the application of several key principles. The measurable electron 'spit out' by the isotope did not have the same energy each emission, which would not align with the principle of the conservation of energy if it was the only particle produced. Thus, physicist Wolfgang Pauli suggested the existence of a non electrically-charged particle which could carry away the remaining decay energy while barely interacting with its surroundings - leading to his hypothesis of the neutrino particle in the 1930s. Further analysis would reveal greater complexity regarding the process of beta decay, where a decay event could be distinguished either as beta-minus decay (producing an antineutrino and electron) and beta-plus decay (producing a neutrino and a positron), altering the identity of the atom and nucleus. Even more considerations arise, such as in the hypothesized case of neutrino-less double beta decay. "There's a proposed idea that a neutrino could act as its own antiparticle, and if a particle and antiparticle come near each other, they annihilate and release energy. So if the neutrino is its own antiparticle, then the neutrinos interacting with themselves would annihilate, and you could see this through certain decays of radioactive isotopes. If that were to happen, it would explain why we have so much matter and so little antimatter in the universe… Because if we had equal parts matter and antimatter in the universe, nothing would be around, because it would have all it would have all annihilated." Mattson explained. Furthermore, with several further layers of classification playing a role in our understanding of these particles, it is important to acknowledge the neutrinos being considered are not all necessarily the same kind of neutrino, with scientists suggesting multiple types or flavors of neutrinos. Neutrinos are a type of uncharged lepton, a broader term for elementary particles that do not experience the strong nuclear force. "There's electron neutrinos, there's muon neutrinos and there's tau neutrinos… one neutrino can have a certain mass, and it can switch between different flavors while it travels through the air." Mattson described. This facet of neutrinos has been previously recognized by the Nobel Prize Committee in 2015, when they awarded the discovery of neutrino oscillations. Neutrino research was also previously awarded in 2002 for scientists who detected cosmic neutrinos from stellar sources including the sun. However, the technology used at the time to measure these oscillations were not fully effective, leaving a discrepancy in their obtained and expected measurements. "They realized that what was happening was the original experiments were only sensitive to one type of neutrino, but a lot of neutrinos from the sun were switching into other types of neutrinos as they made their way to the Earth, and that's why we weren't observing them," Mattson said. This made the improved detection of neutrinos a significant frontier for the future of this research, which brings us to this year's prize-winning IceCube neutrino observatory that is capable of detecting all three flavors. Since neutrinos are neutrally charged and display very minor interactions, neutrino detectors are required to be incredibly large sizes to maximize their chances of interacting with a neutrino - with IceCube being 1 cubic kilometer of Antarctic ice. "The really cool thing about what Ice Cube did is it measured neutrinos from outside not only the solar system, but also from outside the galaxy," Mattson said. "That was groundbreaking because that allows you to now learn about these sources that are super super far away… all these crazy objects like a black hole, like a supernova, like a quasar… So it really made this whole new field of neutrino astronomy [possible], where you don't only have to look at photons… you can now also look at these neutrinos." The very same qualities of neutrinos that were previously discussed become incredibly useful in this context: since these particles barely have any interactions, they can carry an extremely clear representation of far objects relative to particles like photons, which are more likely to experience interfering interactions on the way. "The cool thing about IceCube is if you have a kilometer cube device and you have a particle come in and do its Cherenkov flash, then you're gonna be able to see a couple flashes in a row and trace out a path… that the particle came from… It's not super precise, but it's close enough that you can then… point [telescopes] at it… and then [judge] if there are any possible sources over there." Mattson said. This has been previously demonstrated by IceCube, which has been used to identify sources of high-energy neutrinos from other active galaxies. Now that this technology exists and is already being celebrated by the field, further innovations and advancements are possible. The question arises, what next? "The easy answer is they want to do an IceCube Gen2, which is going to be eight kilometers cubed instead of one kilometer cubed… I think it's fair to assume that this probing [of] the nature of the universe… will lend itself to things that are beneficial to humanity that we can't necessarily predict right now," Mattson concluded.

articles.title: Sexual assault at Hopkins: a survivor's perspective
articles.description: Content warning: This article discusses sexual assault, suicidal thoughts and hospitalization. One night, a friend sent me a news post on Instagram. It was about a Cornell student known publicly as Jane Doe, whose lawsuit alleging she was sexually assaulted at a fraternity had led prosecutors to reopen her case. As I read, a sense of familiarity came over me. Soon my social media was flooded with posts saying "I am Jane Doe." Thousands of people came forward with their own stories of sexual assault on college campuses. Stories of a system that had failed to protect survivors again and again. I decided I would tell mine, too. It begins in 2022, when I was an undergraduate at Hopkins. * * * It was past midnight. I was in the living room of my boyfriend's apartment, working on an assignment while on a call with a friend. My boyfriend was already asleep. The person who assaulted me, whom I'll call S, was drinking in his room with his girlfriend. I thought of them both as friends. Later, S came out and invited me to have a drink with them. It was whiskey, about one shot, and it tasted strange. After the first sip, I felt dizzy and sick, along with an odd sense of excitement, but I finished it. That reaction was unusual for me. I have a fairly high tolerance for alcohol, and I had never reacted to one drink that way. I decided to take a shower. Afterward, I sat on the sofa, waiting to feel clear-headed enough to get back to work. That was when S came out and sexually assaulted me. My friend, still on the phone, told me to go back to my boyfriend's room immediately. I was too shocked to process what had happened. The next morning, I still felt sick, and my friend went with me to the emergency room. I believe they ran a toxicology screen, but nothing was found. Standard screens don't look for every substance. A few days later, I remembered something. A week before that night, S had asked to borrow a few of my sleeping pills, saying he was having trouble sleeping. I gave them to him. I later learned that too much of that medication can cause effects like the ones I had. I have never been able to prove it, but I believe that is what happened. In the days that followed, I was consumed by disgust. I could barely eat. I had flashbacks and intense nightmares. Within a day or two, I reported what happened to the University and began gathering evidence. I spent every day and night thinking about how to make my case and how to make sure he faced consequences. Meanwhile, S kept talking to me as if nothing had happened. He did not seem to think he had done anything wrong. Even after I told him I did not want to speak to him, he kept sending me class notes. Eventually, I could not sleep at all, and I was overwhelmed by suicidal thoughts. After I talked with my friends, they called emergency services, and I was taken to the hospital. I stayed there for several months. The hospitalization placed a heavy financial burden on my family and me. I was forced to take a semester off from school, and even after I left the hospital, I needed extensive treatment. With time, I got better, but the side effects of the medications have permanently affected my health and my ability to function. S went on with his studies. I had to avoid registering for any course he was taking so I would not have to see him. Altogether, my plans were set back a full year. Two days after the assault, I told a professor I trusted what had happened. She listened to me patiently, assured me that I did nothing wrong, and suggested I contact the University's Title IX office to file a report. The next day, I submitted the report through Title IX's online form. Title IX arranged a series of interviews with me. In those first few conversations, before I was hospitalized, I gave them nearly all the information I had. They also interviewed my friends, the other roommates, S's girlfriend and S himself, and they collected evidence. S admitted to assaulting me, but he denied putting anything in my drink. I told Title IX about the sleeping pills and my suspicion about the drink. In the end, they decided it was not enough evidence. Because of my hospitalization, the process was fragmented for me. After I was discharged, I got back in touch with the Title IX office and asked for updates regularly, but the case was delayed again and again. I received the decision five or six months after I left the hospital. Along with it came an investigation report many pages long. I was told I could not show or send it to anyone. S received one semester of probation. Probation? This cannot be, I thought. A student caught cheating on a quiz can receive probation. No trace of it would appear on his transcript or in any public record. For him, it would be as if nothing had happened at all. The only consequence was that if he broke another rule that semester, he would be suspended. He was surely careful enough to stay out of trouble for a few months. I was told I could appeal the decision through a hearing. After more than six months of back and forth, I had nothing left. I did not feel mentally strong enough to go through a hearing, and I decided not to appeal. After the decision, the University issued a no-contact order between us. Another year passed. S had graduated about six months earlier when an email from him arrived in my school inbox. I had blocked him on every social media platform, so he found the one channel I had not. I was in the middle of graduate school application season, already under enormous stress. The moment I saw his name, I was triggered all over again. His email was long. He said he wanted to "clear up the misunderstanding" so that we could "look back on the past with a smile." Most of the email was about him. He wrote that what happened had "affected [him] more than [he] had imagined," that he could not fully focus on his studies or plan for his future, and that he had long been afraid I would hurt him and his family. What he thought "could have been a small matter," he wrote, had "first become a disaster for [me], then gradually eaten away at [his] mental health." He said he felt "surrounded by inexplicable malice." He called what he did to me "that kiss," an "impulsive act" under the influence of alcohol. At the end, he asked me to add him back on social media, so that we could "finally let go of the past." Reading it, I understood that he did not regret what he had done to me. He regretted being caught, and he was afraid I would come after him and damage his future. When I did not reply, he reached out to my mother. He had gotten her contact information while I was in the hospital, when she had come to take care of me. He asked her to persuade me to add him back and listen to what he had to say. Once he graduated, the no-contact order meant nothing. Looking back, there are things I hope the University will change. I hope the process becomes more transparent, so that survivors are kept informed without having to keep asking. I hope investigations can move more quickly. I hope survivors will not have to face the person who assaulted them again in order to appeal a decision. And I hope the consequences for sexual assault will one day reflect what it costs the people who survive it. Four years later, my life has moved forward. I still need treatment and medication to stay mentally stable, and the nightmares and flashbacks still return from time to time. But I was never alone; my friends stood by me throughout. I am now in graduate school, continuing my studies, and I have not let what happened keep me from doing what I love. Only now do I feel ready to write about what happened to me. To anyone going through something similar: Please remember that you are not alone, and please do not blame yourself for what happened. Whether you report it, talk about it or keep it to yourself, that is your choice to make. No choice makes you less of a survivor. What happened to you matters, even if the outcome does not show it. The News-Letter allows parties to withhold the names of parties involved in alleged gender- and sexual-based violence.

articles.title: In my room
articles.description: After an everything shower, a warm, home cooked dinner and a cold poppi poured over ice, the first thing that greets me is the light. Rows of string lights stretch across a 14x12 foot wall, glowing a warm gold. By night, the whole room feels like I'm living inside a lantern. Or maybe, after a long, tiring day, refreshed by my shower routine, I settle into my warm chair with a heat pack to keep me cozy, ready to tackle my homework beneath the comforting glow that surrounds me. Under those lights, the wall is crowded with things I love. NASA posters of stars and the nebulae hang beside Van Gogh's swirling night sky. Van Gogh transports me to a dinner party in a city abroad, bringing liveliness into my otherwise quiet room, while the NASA posters capture a universe that feels so distant and expansive. Both manage to take me somewhere new, bringing faraway destinations to me without requiring me to move. Lower down, a Persian rug runner covers my floor, and a mandala tapestry stretches across the wall. I love the intricate patterns, the way they reflect culture and invite me to meditate. When I lie in bed and trace the swirls and details with my eyes, I find myself becoming absorbed in them, sometimes even losing my place. Even after months of looking at the tapestry, I still discover something new. I've also brought nature into my space, with ivy trailing along the edges of my window. Above my bed, the dreamcatchers are swaying gently, catching my nightmares and leaving me with the promise of a peaceful and restful night's sleep. My dresser is overstuffed, and I'll admit, I can hardly open the third drawer. But on top sit bangles tangled in gold, silver, pink, green, amber and blue; earrings from India; skincare bottles arranged in the order I use them; carefully chosen perfumes of my favorite scents and makeup neatly tucked into my organizer. It might look chaotic to someone else, but I could find anything on there with my eyes closed. Every morning, I get ready here, and every night, I take it all off here. The mirror atop the dresser watches me speak positive affirmations into the world and watches me reflect back to myself after a long day. Then there's my News-Letter shrine, the corner where I keep the writing, clippings, and ideas I don't want to lose. It reminds me of my why and keeps me connected to what I love to do. Besides it, a flower shaped lantern glows on my desk next to pictures of my family. My people are everywhere in this room. There are quotes I've copied out by hand, along with sketches and doodles I've made in the margins of readings during class. To someone else, these things might look like trash, but to me, they're what make my room whole. Together, my walls become a bulletin board of the person I am and the person I hope to become. My bed is a full, piled with too many pillows and too many stuffed animals. Nearly every one was a gift from a friend or family member. I could never explain to a stranger why a slightly squished panda means so much to me, but I remember exactly who gave me each one and when. Every night, as I fall asleep, I'm surrounded by little reminders of the people I love. Even when they're far away, I feel their presence and know how deeply I'm supported. And honestly, it's a shoebox. The room is small enough that I can reach my dresser from my bed. But I've stopped noticing its size. A room doesn't need to be big to be full, and mine is full of light, people, and things I've chosen with intention. When I close the door, the noise from the kitchen, from school, from research, from life itself, begins to fade. The lights cast their gentle glow, and the paintings transport me to distant places. For a few hours, I get to exist somewhere that feels entirely like me. Somewhere familiar, somewhere comforting, somewhere that brings me peace.

articles.title: MIT develops implantable ultrasound device to improve drug delivery to the brain
articles.description: Researchers at the MIT Media Lab have developed an implantable device designed to improve how drugs spread through brain tissue.

articles.title: Scientists use radio waves to flip nuclear spin of single atom in quantum experiment
articles.description: Delft researchers used radio waves to flip a single atom's nuclear spin, revealing an unexpected control mechanism.

articles.title: Dead Planets Orbiting a Dead Star
articles.description: When a star like our Sun reaches its end, it becomes a kind of zombie star called a white dwarf. These bodies have left fusion behind and will radiate only remnant heat for a long, long time. Before they become white dwarfs, they expand, engulf, and destroy any nearby planets. Astronomers have spotted a debris disk around a white dwarf, made from the dust of destroyed planets. Observations show that two new resurrected planets have formed in this disk, creating dead planets orbiting a dead star.

articles.title: Double debris disk orbiting a dead star hints at our solar system's future
articles.description: Astronomers using the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope (ESO's VLT) have found a rare disk of debris around a dead star that provides a glimpse of what may happen to our solar system. Unlike in similar systems previously found, the debris—the leftovers of planets that once orbited the star—is organized in a double disk, the two parts separated by a clear gap. The disk appears to be shaped by two planetary bodies, one possibly as big as Pluto, that have survived the violent death of the star.

articles.title: Narcissism May Be a Spectrum, and Those with Grandiose Narcissism Process Social Embarrassment Differently
articles.description: Learn how brain-imaging showed how people with stronger narcissistic traits respond differently when someone else’s social standing is threatened.

articles.title: New cacao variety could help protect global chocolate supply from disease
articles.description: Chocolate lovers may not realize it, but the future of one of the world's most popular foods is increasingly under pressure. Diseases, shifting weather patterns and other environmental stressors are threatening cacao production globally, contributing to supply concerns and economic challenges for the millions of farmers who grow the crop that makes chocolate possible.

articles.title: Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS Has Dusty Ice Grains Unlike Those in Most Comets, but Similar to Frozen Worlds Beyond Neptune
articles.description: Learn more about the unique ice grains from comet 3I/ATLAS and how they may hold clues to the building blocks of planets.

articles.title: Scientists uncover new way to control magnetism and topology using light in atomically thin materials
articles.description: Envision a material whose magnetic properties and electronic topology can be toggled by exposure to light, paving the way for future electronic devices that do not rely on traditional electrical switching, which wastes energy by producing heat.

articles.title: Extreme risk protection orders are designed to prevent gun violence. But how do they impact the people subject to them?
articles.description: About 125 people die from gun violence through homicide or suicide in the United States every day. Many more are injured by firearms. Extreme risk protection orders (ERPOs), known in California as gun violence restraining orders, are designed to keep firearms temporarily away from people at risk of harming themselves or others.

articles.title: Potential antimalarial compound discovered in institute's microbe collection
articles.description: Scientists hunting for a new malaria treatment may have found a solution within a historical natural compound collection housed at The Herbert Wertheim UF Scripps Institute for Biomedical Innovation & Technology.

articles.title: An Ancient Pandemic Left a Gene Silent in Chimpanzees, Which May Offer Clues as to Why Their Brains Differ From Ours
articles.description: Learn how an ancient virus silenced a gene that helps young human nerve cells grow, leaving a lasting difference between our closest relatives and us.

articles.title: Light-controlled brake makes random molecular motion 300,000 times slower
articles.description: Molecules are never still. Driven by thermal energy, they are constantly moving through space, while their individual parts also rotate relative to one another. Scientists at IOCB Prague have now shown that random motion within a molecule can be dramatically suppressed. Using light, they can slow down the relative rotation of two different parts of a single molecule by up to five orders of magnitude, paving the way for more complex molecular machines.

articles.title: Technician cracks 1,600-year-old mystery to replicate color-changing effect of Roman glass masterpiece
articles.description: The Lycurgus Cup, a world-renowned 4th-century A.D. artifact housed in the British Museum, is constructed of "dichroic" glass that shifts from jade green in reflected light to ruby red in transmitted light. This means that depending on where the light source is positioned, observers can see the cup displayed in two distinctive, contrasting colors.

articles.title: ‘Mosquito toilets’: How scientists are using mosquito poop to detect viruses
articles.description: Researchers have developed a “mosquito toilet” — a tool to analyse mosquito waste for pathogens — that could be an early warning system for emerging health threats.

articles.title: The mathematics of growing a shell—recreating diverse mollusk shells with just three inputs
articles.description: Kaushik Bhattacharya is an engineer and materials scientist, but he has always been fascinated by seashells. Part of the draw is the "beautiful" idea that even simple organisms like mollusks can construct wonderfully complex structures over and over again, even in differing environments. He marvels at nature's engineering capabilities.

articles.title: These Analysts Boost Their Forecasts On Agilysys After Upbeat Q3 Results
Skeleton of Nanotyrannus ‘Jodi,’ T. Rex’s Cousin, Is Auctioned for $47.3 Million
articles.description: The Nanotyrannus specimen is the latest dinosaur fossil to fetch a high price at a private auction, this time at Sotheby’s.

articles.title: STAT+: Nonprofit resurrects shelved gene therapy after startup shuts down
articles.description: Last year, U.K. gene therapy startup Bloomsbury Genetic Therapies announced it was shutting down after dosing just one patient. Now, a nonprofit is resurrecting its lead program:

articles.title: Brambles are a problem weed in South Africa but researchers are closer to finding a natural enemy to manage them
articles.description: Biological control looks like a feasible option for managing invasive brambles.

articles.title: Anyone Can Dock: Molecular docking platform brings protein-binding predictions to smartphones, tablets and computers
articles.description: A new platform, developed by researchers at the Center for Computational Sciences, University of Tsukuba, in collaboration with Mahidol University, makes molecular docking easier to access, understand, and integrate into experimental research. The work is published in the Journal of Cheminformatics.

articles.title: Want to be happier? Oxford research says ask yourself these 3 questions
articles.description: What does it take to be happy? Three simple and surprising questions may hold the answer, research found. While most of us seek more money and greater achievement as paths to happiness, these questions are all about connection. They’re more strongly associated with self-measured life satisfaction than either money or success. That’s according to the 2025 World Happiness Report published by Oxford University and based on a study of people in 147 countries. The questions are: How often do you eat meals with other people, rather than alone? Do you generally expect strangers to be kind and trustworthy? How often do you do things for other people, such as making donations, volunteering, or helping strangers? This may all sound like wishful thinking, but the research shows that, while economic security and career satisfaction contribute to happiness, these prosocial factors make a much bigger difference. If you want to be happy, 1. Eat with others This is a rare instance where the report’s happiness advice coincides with frequently offered success advice to never have lunch alone. Lunching at your desk can mean missing out on valuable opportunities for networking or relationship building. It turns out it can also mean missing the chance to be happier by building a stronger social connection. Research suggests that we often expect spending time alone will make us happier than being with others, especially people we don’t know well. But then when we do spend time with others, it makes us happier than we expected. The research looked at whether subjects ate with others or alone for lunch and dinner (it didn’t consider breakfast). Happiness appeared to peak at a whopping 13 lunches or dinners with others per week, which is more meal sharing than most Americans do. But it showed that any amount of eating with others will increase your happiness. So go ahead and grab yourself a lunch or dinner date, even if the person you invite isn’t a valuable business connection. It will make you feel more connected, and boost your happiness, too. 2. Expect strangers to be trustworthy If you dropped your wallet on the street, how likely is it that someone would return it to you with the money still inside? World Happiness Report researchers found that most people underestimate how often they would get their wallets back in this scenario. They also found that those who thought the wallet return was likelier also tended to be happier. But while eating with others would be an excellent business practice, trusting strangers probably isn’t. In a world where not every stranger is trustworthy, how do you balance the benefits of trusting strangers against the very real risks of trusting the wrong one? But consider how many breakout companies are built on the outlandish idea that you can indeed trust strangers. Amazon, Facebook, Etsy, eBay, and other online marketplaces let strangers buy and sell from each other. Uber, Rover, and other such companies encourage us to put our safety, or that of our beloved pets, into the hands of people we’ve never met. Why do we trust these strangers? Because other strangers left reviews saying we could. It seems illogical and yet it works. Does this mean you should blindly accept business propositions from people you don’t know without any due diligence? Of course not. You also should not leave your wallet in the street and assume someone will bring it back to you. But if you tend to automatically distrust anyone you don’t know, try to change that mindset. It will make you happier. It might make the people you do business with happier too. 3. Be kind to others The report looked at three types of benevolent acts: donating, volunteering, and helping strangers. “The well-being benefits of benevolent acts depend on why and how people engage in them. Both helpers and recipients experience greater happiness from caring and sharing when they do so in the context of caring connections, choice, and clear positive impact,” the researchers write. For one thing, choice is important. If you hear about a disaster in your area and feel inspired to make a donation to help, that’s likelier to make you happy than, say, feeling compelled to donate to a charity because your biggest customer or your boss has asked you to. And both giver and receiver of a benevolent act benefit more when they can see a clear positive impact. If you make a donation or volunteer your time to help rebuild a local park, and then spend time there watching people enjoy the park, you’ll get a bigger happiness boost. If the people there know you helped out and can thank you, they will too. Performing benevolent acts gets you the biggest happiness result for the smallest effort. Being kind to other people doesn’t just make you happy, it makes them happy too, World Happiness Report researchers found. That may inspire those people to their own acts of kindness, inspiring others to be kind, and so on. Pretty soon, you might have a self-perpetuating happiness machine. That could benefit any organization or community. —Minda Zetlin This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com. Inc. is the voice of the American entrepreneur. We inspire, inform, and document the most fascinating people in business: the risk-takers, the innovators, and the ultra-driven go-getters that represent the most dynamic force in the American economy.

articles.title: Will a new strategy help protect Northern Ireland's nature?
articles.description: About 40% of the plants and animals in protected sites across Northern Ireland fall short of meeting the standard for "favourable condition".
